description:
Fifty days into the migrant crisis in the Spanish territory of Ceuta, up to 10,000 people remain stranded, nearly half of them without shelter, grouped on the beach under armed police and made to wait for food. Migrant Otman Taussi says police grab and beat those who try to stand up while queuing.

Five-year-old Ali made a Spanish flag in the camp for the country he hopes to call home. Instead, his family says he was shot with a pellet gun by anti-immigration protesters trying to force migrants back to Morocco.

The humanitarian crisis has become a political one, with pressure mounting on Madrid to find a solution and on the European Union to strengthen its external borders. There are rumours of another surge at the border, with a march planned from the Moroccan side to "liberate Ceuta," prompting police and military reinforcements. For years, Donald Trump has insisted the US needs Greenland for national security. Now he says he has struck a deal for permanent control of the Arctic island's security, announcing on social media that it addresses all of Washington's concerns.

Trump first floated acquiring the island in his first term, calling it essentially a real estate deal. The US has had a military presence there since the 1940s, and Greenland played a vital role for NATO in monitoring Soviet forces during the Cold War. A 1951 defence pact granted Washington rights to build bases there, later scaled back in 2004.

The deal's details remain undisclosed and are expected to emerge when it is signed next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Al Jazeera's Michael Appel reports.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
A 1967 treaty is supposed to keep outer space peaceful, but a growing space race between global powers is raising questions about what countries can actually send up there. Alex Baird explains what the law allows.

The Outer Space Treaty, signed in 1967 and now joined by 118 countries including Russia, the US and China, was designed to promote the peaceful exploration of space. It bans nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction from Earth's orbit and outer space, and prohibits military bases, weapons testing and military exercises on the moon and other celestial bodies. It also bars any country from claiming ownership over space or celestial bodies.

But the treaty has gaps: it does not prohibit conventional weapons from being placed in Earth's orbit, leaving room for capabilities such as space-based communication jammers or anti-satellite weapons.

Al Jazeera's Alex Baird reports from Washington, DC.

title: What international law says about weapons in space, and its gaps

description:
Most voting in the US midterm elections will take place on November 3, with the outcome determining which party controls Congress and much of President Donald Trump's agenda for his final two years in office. Patty Culhane explains how the process actually works.

The US constitution gives states the power to run federal elections, so every state sets its own rules. In Virginia, South Dakota and Minnesota, voters can already cast early ballots in person. In California and Ohio, early voting cannot start until 29 days before the election, while Alabama, Mississippi and New Hampshire only allow voting in person on election day itself.

States also differ on mail and absentee voting, which lets people who cannot get to the polls, including disabled voters and deployed service members, request, complete and mail in a ballot. 

Al Jazeera's Patty Culhane explains.

Richard Weitz, a senior fellow at the NATO Defense College and security analyst with Wikistrat, says the new US-Denmark Greenland security deal is being hailed by Trump supporters as a diplomatic win, even though it falls well short of the president's earlier ambition to fully control the territory.

Weitz says this fits a pattern: Trump has also floated annexing Canada, the Panama Canal and Venezuela, but has repeatedly backed down in the face of local opposition and settled for less. In Greenland's case, he says, Trump secured almost everything he wanted except formal annexation.

Most importantly, Weitz says, the agreement defuses a major source of tension within NATO that dominated Trump's first term, freeing the alliance to focus on Russia's conventional threat to Ukraine and hybrid, political and subversive threats to NATO members, including a recent report that Russia hired criminals to assassinate dissidents in the US.

title: Trump got almost everything but annexation in Greenland deal: Analysis

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Voters in heavily Democratic northern Virginia are casting their ballots early, part of a broader national shift in how Americans vote. In 2024, 32 percent of voters cast ballots early in person, up from 21 percent in the 2022 midterms, according to Pew Research Center.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly questioned voting by mail, and his administration has sought new restrictions on mail ballots, though the Supreme Court has blocked those restrictions from taking effect for these midterms. 

But access is just one issue on voters' minds. Many cite the economy and cost of living, while some voice strong opposition to the US war in Iran and its sanctions. Even in this Democratic stronghold, Republican voters back the administration's policies on taxes, regulation and government spending, with some saying they are embracing early voting for the first time.

Al Jazeera's Eva McKend reports from Arlington, Virginia.

title: Early voting rises in Virginia amid fight over Trump's mail ballot limits

description:
Google has confirmed to Al Jazeera the latest instance in which an artificial intelligence model has hacked into a company. Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, says the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it believed were part of a test. In all three known instances, she says, the model stopped short of completing the hack.

Al Jazeera's John Hendren reports from Los Angeles.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Five female students at the Autonomous University of Morelos have been killed in the last 18 months, sparking fear and mourning across the campus in central Mexico. The most recent victim, Claudia Tacoronte, a 21-year-old exchange student from Spain, had been in the country just a month when authorities say she was stabbed during an attempted robbery. A suspect has been detained. 

President Claudia Sheinbaum says her government is bringing down the overall murder rate, including in Morelos. But students say they take daily precautions to protect themselves, from sharing their location with family to photographing what they're wearing before leaving home, hoping they won't have to mourn another classmate.

Al Jazeera's John Holman reports from Mexico City.
